cognate_refs.locus: Vǫlsungakviða in forna 9 (= Helgakviða Hundingsbana II 9; FJ 1926)

notes: Candidate from the Phase 8c reader study (docs/research/8c-results.md): an addition to a known formula, not a new formula, and unconfirmed by an expert. Known: only the compound 'raw-eater' (Gk ὠμηστής = Ved. āmā́d-, West 2007 ch. 2 p. 80 with n. 16) and the word equations. The candidate is the free clause *h₂eh₃mó- + *kréwh₂s + *h₁ed-. Greek has it in one clause: Il. 22.347 ὤμ̓ … κρέα ἔδμεναι, Achilles wishing to eat Hector's flesh raw (checked in AGDT). There ὠμά agrees with κρέα but is predicative ('eat the flesh raw'). Vedic has it split: in AVŚ 8.6.23 (DCS sentence 'AVŚ, 8, 6.s48', stanza counter 23; checked) ya āmaṃ māṃsam adanti pauruṣeyaṃ ca ye kraviḥ, demons 'who eat raw meat, and who [eat] human gore'. So āmám qualifies māṃsám (not in the line) and kravíḥ is the second object of the same verb. The exact NP āmá- + kravís- stands in RV 1.162.10b āmásya kravíṣaḥ ('the smell of the raw flesh'; genitive, no verb; checked in VedaWeb). Old Norse (checked in FJ 1926) keeps eta and has hrátt, a *krewh₂- derivative 'raw' in place of *h₂eh₃mó-; the noun is renewed (kjöt). It counts for the verb only. Morphology: the athematic root present *h₁éd-/h₁d- of Ved. adánti (3pl; the lemma is cited as atti, the Sanskrit citation form of that present, so the check can find it) and of the Homeric athematic infinitive ἔδμεναι. 3pl and singular kréwh₂s follow the AV; Greek has the plural κρέα. The lexicon glosses kréwh₂s 'blood', but its reflexes here mean raw flesh or gore (kravís-), meat (κρέας) and gore (Lat. cruor); hence 'raw flesh'. Support only: the raw-eater compounds (Il. 11.454 ὠμησταί tearing corpses; RV 10.87.7d āmā́daḥ … adantu) and Od. 9.297 κρέ̓ ἔδων of the Cyclops (no 'raw'). Generic risk is real (three basic words), but the contexts agree: savage or demonic eating of human flesh.

Candidate from the Phase 8c reader study (docs/research/8c-results.md): an addition to a known formula, not a new formula, and unconfirmed by an expert. Known: the word equations amŕ̥ta- = ἄμβροτος and vas- = ἕννυμι. West 2007 ch. 3 n. 126 discusses ἄμβροτα εἵματα of Sarpedon's corpse (Il. 16.680), and ch. 2 has *wes- with other coverings ('clothed in a cloud', nábho vásānaḥ ~ νεφέλην ἕσσαντο). The new element is the Vedic witness. RV 6.75.18b (= AVŚ 7.118.1, both checked) sómas tvā rā́jāmŕ̥tenā́nu vastām: 'let King Soma clothe you with the immortal', said over the warrior's armour. AVŚ 9.1.1 (DCS sentence s2, stanza counter 1; checked) has amṛ́taṃ vásānām, 'wearing the immortal'. The Greek is the stock line περὶ δ̓ ἄμβροτα εἵματα ἕσσε(ν), all checked: Il. 16.670 (imperative, Zeus to Apollo; AGDT mislemmatizes ἕσσον as ἵζω), Il. 16.680, Od. 24.59, and Hymn. Hom. 6.6 in glaux. Drift: Greek puts ἄμβροτος on the garment noun εἵματα (*wésmn̥, Greek only), while Vedic uses the substantivized neuter amŕ̥tam as the covering. The line follows the Vedic instrumental. Greek has the instrumental of a derivative beside it in the same lines: χρῖσε … ἀμβροσίῃ, 'anointed with ambrosia'. The verb is shared at root level only: Vedic has the root present (vastām, 3sg middle imperative used transitively), Greek the s-aorist (ἕσσον, ἕσσε). The engine's only *wes- 'clothe' lexeme is the nasal present *wes-néw- of ἕννυμι, which neither passage has. The builder's Greek 'exact' rests on the lemma ἕννυμι only. The lexicon has no root present *wés-tor (pie-lex-westi-2 is *wes- 'sell'). The imperative mood is shared (Il. 16.670, RV 6.75.18b). Person and active voice follow Il. 16.670 (2sg); the Vedic is 3sg middle. The object 'him' is interpolated: Sarpedon is implicit in the Greek, and the Vedic has tvā 'you'. The lexeme's gloss 'dress oneself' is the middle; the active is 'clothe someone', as with ἕννυμι.

West 2007 ch. 2 p. 84: Vedic svādór … mádhvaḥ 'of the sweet mead' = Homeric μέθυ ἡδύ, with μέθυ shifted to 'wine' (also Schmitt 1967 §529). The NP *swéh₂dus médʰu is the formula. RV 1.84.10a-b svādór itthā́ viṣūváto mádhvaḥ pibanti, 'they drink of the sweet mead' (checked in VedaWeb). The Greek μέθυ ἡδύ recurs as a line-end formula (nine times in the Odyssey: Od. 9.162, 10.184, 17.533 and others; checked in AGDT). The Old English witness swētne medo, 'the sweet mead' repaid by retainers (Finnsburh 39, checked in the Gutenberg Beowulf appendix), is the 8c Stage A addition (8c-results.md: West and Schmitt cite Vedic and Greek only). OE swēte continues the u-stem *swōtu- moved into the ja-stems, so the builder's 'exact' for it is generous: formation level. The engine cannot realize a verbless NP (one V slot per clause), so the NP stands as the subject of an interpolated existential copula, which keeps it attributive as in all three branches. The frames differ and none is shared: Vedic pibanti 'drink' (the reduplicated present *pí-ph₃-e-, which the lexicon cannot inflect), Greek δαινύμενοι 'feasting' (Od. 9.162) and ἔδουσιν 'eat' (Od. 17.533), OE forgyldan 'repay'. The cases differ too: Vedic partitive genitive, Greek and OE accusative; the nominative is the copula's. RV 8.49.4b mádhvaḥ svā́diṣṭham has the superlative (root level) and is not cited. Generic risk: a honey drink is naturally sweet, but the pairing is a fixed formula in Greek and is claimed as inherited by West. Old English swētne medo (Finnsburh 39) is Ettmüller's emendation; the manuscript reads hwitne 'white' (tier2 review r3): kept as support only.

Phase 8c Stage A claim C048 (accepted; 8c-results.md: 'partly known', not one of the three final candidates). West 2007 ch. 3 p. 158 with n. 127 has only the motif: the gods' horses are immortal, Greek and Iranian. Durante 1976, which we do not hold, may already have the lexical match. Unconfirmed by an expert. AVŚ 13.1.24 (DCS sentence s47, stanza counter 24; checked): sū́ryasyā́śvā hárayaḥ ketumántaḥ sádā vahanty amṛ́tāḥ sukháṃ rátham, 'the Sun's bay horses always draw, immortal, the easy-running chariot'. Il. 16.380-381 = 16.866-867 (checked in AGDT): ὠκέες ἵπποι | ἄμβροτοι, οὓς Πηλῆϊ θεοὶ δόσαν, Achilles' god-given horses. In both, n̥mr̥tó- stands in apposition to the plural horse noun ('the horses, immortal …'). The engine cannot build a verbless NP, so the line renders the apposition as a predicate with an interpolated copula (h₁sénti). Generic risk is medium: 'immortal' is freely applied to divine things in both traditions. The line's 'swift' (ὠκέες) belongs to the separate swift-horses formula (divine-twins-004) and is not used. Hymn. Hom. 2.375-376 (renewed ἀθανάτους) is not cited.
